title: Uncut Gems

facts: Score for the Safdie brothers' 2019 film, released by Warp on 13 December 2019, 17 tracks, about 52 minutes
Produced by Lopatin; recorded at Electric Garden and Gaia Studios in Brooklyn
Josh Safdie first cut the film to a temp score of library and new age music before Lopatin wrote original pieces
Built around a Moog One synthesizer plus Omnisphere; saxophone, flute and choir also used; Eli Keszler drums on two tracks
Choral production by Conor Abbott Brown, mixing by Matt Cohn; film dialogue intercut on some tracks
Named touchstones: Isao Tomita, Tangerine Dream, Vangelis, Emerald Web; one track reworks Haydn's Symphony No. 88, another nods to the Akira theme
Metacritic 74; peaked at 44 on the UK soundtrack chart
Moog Music and Lopatin made a behind the scenes video on the score
Lopatin worked by trial and error on the Moog One, keeping accidents that worked; 1970s analog psychedelia as a reference
Released the same day the film opened in US cinemas, on Warp
Second Safdie score after Good Time (2017), which won the Cannes soundtrack award
Credited to his birth name rather than Oneohtrix Point Never, unlike Good Time (per search snippet)

title: Leadbelly's Last Sessions Volume One

facts: Recorded fall 1948 over three evenings (late September, October, November) in jazz writer Frederic Ramsey Jr.'s New York apartment, about a year before Lead Belly died on 6 December 1949
Probably his only commercial recordings made on magnetic tape; the long reels kept his spoken introductions and talk between songs
Aim was to record his whole repertoire; the LPs keep the songs in the order sung, mostly without bands between them
First evening he had no guitar with him, so he sang unaccompanied hollers, field calls, spirituals; his wife Martha joined some choruses
Charles Edward Smith attended the second evening; the third ended with 'Leaving Blues' and Ramsey never saw him again
Ramsey refused to license the tapes to any label that would not issue them complete and in sequence; only Moses Asch's Folkways agreed
Original issue: Folkways FP 241 / 242 (later 2941 / 2942), notes from 1953 by Ramsey and Asch; Peter Bartok prepared the 1953 production masters
Some tape began to peel soon after recording; first evening used a small vocal microphone, later evenings a dynamic microphone; drapes used to damp the room
1994 Smithsonian Folkways CD reissue (SF 40068 to 40071) adds two unissued songs; notes by Anthony Seeger, Jeff Place, Matt Walters, Sean Killeen
Posthumous discography lists Lead Belly's Last Sessions, recorded late 1948 in New York, his only commercial recording on magnetic tape
Legacy section: Kurt Cobain listed Last Session Vol. 1 among the 50 albums most influential on Nirvana's sound
Library record: sessions dated 27 September, 15 October and 5 November 1948 at Ramsey's home
Library record dates Volume 1 to Folkways 1953, reissued 1957 and 1962

example_line: Recorded on tape over three evenings in 1948 at Frederic Ramsey's New York home, a year before Lead Belly died.
example_line_sources: Smithsonian Folkways liner notes SFW40068 (Seeger intro, Ramsey 1953 essay)
Lead Belly en Wikipedia, posthumous discography
notes: No album article; the Lead Belly article has a short mention plus the Cobain fact. The Smithsonian liner notes PDF is very rich (Ramsey's 1953 first person account). folkways.si.edu album page returned 403; the PDF text was extracted locally. Release year sources disagree (1953 vs 1954).

title: 加爾基 精液 栗ノ花 (Kalk samen kuri no hana)

facts: Third studio album, 23 February 2003, Toshiba EMI / Virgin; first released on copy controlled CD, normal CD in 2008
Produced by 'Bakeneko Killer', a pseudonym for Sheena and engineer Uni Inoue; her first fully self produced major release
Recorded at Toshiba EMI studio, Studio Terra, Tokyo Opera City Concert Hall and a ryokan in Atami, by overdubbing one instrument at a time on a Mac
Working title was 'Wonderful, Vulgar, Eccentric'; the final title came from staff arguing about what semen smells like
Lead single 'Stem' was her first Oricon number one; a companion short film Kaleidoscope came out a month earlier
Ranked second in a 2009 CNN Asia list of overlooked 2000s Japanese music
Track order, booklet and instrumentation of paired songs are symmetric around the sixth track 'Kuki'; running time edited to 44:44
Vocals recorded in a wooden room of an Atami inn; a plan to record in Germany was dropped
Seiji Kameda, her usual arranger, did not take part; two songs were left off for not fitting the concept
Booklet uses old kanji and historical kana spelling; vinyl bonus track written by guitarist Ukigumo
Student newspaper retrospective review (2025) focused on the sound, e.g. vocal processing on the opening track

title: Danger Money

facts: Second and last studio album; released 16 March 1979 on E.G. / Polydor
Recorded November 1978 to January 1979 at AIR Studios, London; produced by Eddie Jobson and John Wetton
Trio of Jobson (keyboards, violin), Wetton (bass, vocals), Terry Bozzio (drums); Bill Bruford and Allan Holdsworth had played early versions of three songs on the 1978 tour
Wetton brought in most of 'Nothing to Lose' and wrote its lyrics; Jobson's CS80 solo on 'Rendezvous 6:02' stacks all 16 oscillators
Reached 45 on the US Billboard 200; remastered in the 2016 Ultimate Collector's Edition box
Band article covers the lineup change from quartet to trio
Holdsworth left over creative differences and Bruford followed; American drummer Bozzio joined
Song themes: a hitman on the title track, a train to Waterloo in 'Rendezvous 6:02', Las Vegas in 'Caesar's Palace Blues'; 'Carrying No Cross' is the 12 minute closer
Box set includes Jobson and Wetton interviews from New York 1978 and London 1979 (search snippet)

example_line: Made as a trio after Bruford and Holdsworth left, it was recorded at AIR Studios in London from late 1978.
